newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-SPAIN'S OLD FIRM CLASH IS MORE THAN JUST A GAME.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-SPAIN'S OLD FIRM CLASH IS MORE THAN JUST A GAME.

text.p: If there's one league fixture in Spain that is more than just a game, then that game is the old firm clash between Real Madrid and Barcelona.
Far more than just a sporting contest -- and arguably Europe's biggest club game -- Real-Barca fixtures are a clash of ideologies, histories, and even languages.

The two meet in the league on Saturday and whereas Real have long been identified with the intolerant centralism of the Spanish right, Barcelona are the standard bearers of Catalonia, Spain's most vigorously independent region.
It's a potent mixture in a country that is effectively a collection of separate nations welded together under rule from Madrid.
And the tensions are not just past history.

With Civil War victor and dogmatic centralist General Franco -- himself a well-known Real Madrid fan -- now over 20 years dead, debate is raging over just how much power the regions should take back from Madrid.
Not surprisingly there have been suggestions that Catalonia and the Basque Country should have their own 'national' teams.
Until they do -- and FIFA rules would have to be bent for that to happen -- the best comparison with Real-Madrid Barcelona would not be a club game, but England vs Scotland.
For the Spanish public the effect is intoxicating, and very few people in the country are left neutral.
"I'm not going to waste my time watching football, but Real-Barca is different," says Seville engineer Juan Luis.
The game routinely breaks seasonal television viewing figures.
Weddings are re-arranged so as not to have guests sneaking off to find a television to watch the big game.

Spanish sports dailies have dedicated six or more pages each day for over a week to the big clash. Readers can enjoy players' diaries, opinions of famous fans, a review of previous games between the sides, the usual pre-match interviews and a bundle of trivia.

Journalists even treated fans to a league table of cars driven by the leading players -- with the 81 million peseta ($642,000) collection driven by Real's starting line-up pipping Barcelona's at the post.
Exhaustive media coverage of the game has led Atletico Madrid players to complain about the lack of attention given to Wednesday's Champion League game against Widzew Lodz.
"It's a lot of gas about mediocre teams," said outspoken Atletico president Jesus Gil.
One female television presenter began the sports section of her bulletin with a weary reference to 'the new game of the century'.
The repercussions of a one-sided game are just as great.

Graffiti reading simply '5-0' appeared all over Madrid after Brazilian striker Romario led Barcelona's drubbing of the old rivals in January 1994. A year later the score was reversed, and the same graffiti appeared overnight in Barcelona.
Management at Spain's 'grandees' know that a good result in the old firm games can salvage a season.
Former Barcelona coach Johan Cruyff nearly lost his job early in the 1989-90 season, but was saved by a 3-1 win over Real, and recovered to lead Barcelona to four consecutive league titles.
Most importantly for Barca fans, Cruyff also took the club's first European Cup, a trophy that Real had won six times.
Cruyff was also at the centre of probably the most famous Barcelona victory ever -- the 1974 5-0 drubbing of Real in Madrid.
Remarkably, several years later, the Madrid-based Spanish national television company announced that it had lost the footage of the game.
